title: Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt Check/Revision (TIPS)
summary: TIPS check/revision guidance for stenosis or occlusion, recurrent variceal bleeding or ascites, elevated portosystemic gradient, shunt dysfunction on Doppler ultrasound, and over-correction.

Contraindications depend on the goal: encephalopathy/heart failure may indicate shunt reduction rather than prohibit revision.
Avoid increasing shunt flow in uncontrolled encephalopathy, decompensated heart failure, or severe pulmonary hypertension.
Uncontrolled infection or severe hepatic decompensation requires individualized multidisciplinary review.

Discuss the expected benefit, alternatives, and patient-specific risks. This risk summary supports the discussion and institutional consent form; it is not an exhaustive consent document.
assess portal-vein patency, the uncovered portal end, and inflow into the shunt.
look for underexpansion, kink, focal stenosis, thrombus, or incomplete tract coverage.
the hepatic vein-IVC junction is a common site of edge stenosis and intimal hyperplasia.
calculate the gradient from main portal pressure to a consistent systemic reference at the free hepatic vein or IVC.
persistent varices can maintain bleeding risk; large spontaneous shunts can worsen encephalopathy.
chronic occlusion or severe angulation may require transhepatic or transsplenic access for through-and-through control.
review symptoms, Doppler and prior imaging, stent type and diameter, and earlier gradients.
select the hepatic end from the IJ and secure a wire in the portal system.
perform venography from portal inflow through the stent and hepatic outflow; identify focal lesions and collaterals.
record portal and free hepatic vein or IVC pressures before treatment using one systemic reference.
angioplasty a focal lesion; reline or extend recurrent, resistant, intrastent, or edge disease.
clear thrombus, then fix the stenosis, kink, or uncovered segment that caused it.
expand incrementally, improve inflow or outflow, and selectively embolize persistent high-risk varices when indicated.
after medical optimization, use a controlled hourglass, parallel, or tapered reduction rather than routine complete occlusion.
repeat portography and pressures; document final flow, gradient, branch preservation, and no extravasation.
abnormal velocity raises suspicion but is not the final diagnosis; correlate with symptoms, venography, and direct pressure measurements.
switching between right atrial, free hepatic, and IVC pressure can create a false gradient change; use the same reference before and after revision.
confirm the wire is intraluminal and maintain stable portal purchase before ballooning, thrombectomy, or relining.

items.strong: Clearing thrombus without fixing the cause:

items: untreated edge stenosis, kink, underexpansion, or poor inflow and outflow invites rapid rethrombosis.
avoid covering major portal branches or adjacent hepatic-vein drainage and avoid unnecessary extension into the IVC or right atrium.
liberated thrombus can pass directly to the pulmonary circulation; monitor hemodynamics and use an appropriate clot-management strategy.
too much narrowing restores bleeding or ascites; too little may not improve encephalopathy or cardiac overload. Recheck flow and gradient after each adjustment.
transhepatic or transsplenic rescue adds capsular bleeding risk; plan tract closure and confirm hemostasis.

items: Regular diet, timed vitals, Tylenol, IJ and femoral access recovery, 1-hour discharge, AVS, and TIPS ultrasound/clinic follow-up.

blocks.title: Routine orders
items: Regular diet.
Vital signs every 15 minutes x 4.
Tylenol 650 mg PRN.

blocks.title: Access care
items: Elevate HOB >45 degrees x 1 hour.
Bedrest with leg flat for 2 hours.

blocks.title: Anticoagulation to resume
items: Warfarin: resume the day after the procedure; bridging requires individualized multidisciplinary planning.
IV unfractionated heparin: 6-8 hours after the procedure.
Enoxaparin: 12 hours after the procedure.
Apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, and edoxaban: Table 6 lists 24 hours; confirm renal function and local policy before restarting.
Clopidogrel: 6 hours after the procedure for a 75-mg dose or 24 hours for a 300-600-mg loading dose.
Ticagrelor, prasugrel, and aspirin: resume the day after the procedure.
Restart only after procedural bleeding risk is controlled; traumatic, neuraxial, multi-agent, and high-thrombosis-risk cases need individualized review.
